sessions.title: Is there a scientific method?
sessions.question: Is hypothesis-testing a universal account of inquiry, a standard for justification, or one useful mode among several?
reading: Read Platt in full. Identify the role of alternative explanations and discriminating observations.
Read Cleland’s Geology paper in full. It makes the argument in four pages, for geologists; the discussant brings the rest.
Discussant: the 2002 Philosophy of Science paper develops the same argument in full, with the time-asymmetry argument and the reply to the charge that historical science is inferior.
sessions.contrast: Platt offers a prescriptive strategy; Cleland analyzes differences between experimental interventions and reconstructing past events. Neither paper directly records this group’s daily research. Test both against an actual project rather than declaring one a complete scientific method.
prompts: Can an observational study discriminate hypotheses without controlling the system?
Which research actions are not well described as a test?
Are we describing how ideas are generated or how claims are warranted?
sessions.prep: Bring one important paper and a short reconstruction of how the work actually proceeded. Mark which steps are documented and which are inferred.
sessions.exercise: Reconstruct a project as initial knowledge -> observation -> representation -> question -> proposed explanation -> check. Compare that trajectory with the published narrative. Do not invent a private chronology from the article structure.
sessions.output: Inquiry-action vocabulary v1: exploration, measurement, characterization, question formation, explanation, discrimination, synthesis, and revision. Note where an agent should abstain or seek more evidence.
sessions.audit: Retain the original pair, but explicitly distinguish methodological arguments from evidence about research practice.

sessions.title: Exploratory experimentation is not theory-free
sessions.question: What makes exploration systematic when a hypothesis or even the relevant concepts are not yet stable?
reading: Read Steinle’s full short paper. The original publication is 1997; later online posting is not a second publication year.
Read Karaca’s introduction and concluding discussion. A discussant selects one high-energy-physics case; the entire long article is optional.
sessions.contrast: Steinle reconstructs exploratory experimental work. Karaca distinguishes ways theory enters exploratory and theory-directed experiments. Together they resist both a hypothesis-first caricature and the opposite claim that observations are theory-free.
prompts: Which assumptions are needed to operate and interpret an instrument?
When does changing a representation amount to changing a concept?
How should an agent record an exploratory action without retroactively inventing a hypothesis?
sessions.prep: Choose a small unfamiliar dataset or laboratory output. Withhold a target hypothesis, but provide provenance and relevant safety constraints.
sessions.exercise: Independently log the next five actions you would take. Compare inspection, plotting, variation of conditions, calibration, literature consultation, and anomaly follow-up. Tag assumptions rather than pretending the actions start from no prior knowledge.
sessions.output: Exploration policy v1: allowed actions, their information purpose, assumptions, evidence retained, and criteria for switching to hypothesis discrimination.
sessions.audit: Complete the Steinle citation and add a genuine qualification from Karaca rather than leaving a one-paper session.

sessions.title: From coastal traces to earthquake histories
sessions.question: When do geological traces discriminate a causal history, and when can different processes produce similar deposits?
reading: Read Atwater in full.
Read Nelson and colleagues’ abstract, discussion of diagnostic criteria, and conclusions; the discussant examines the detailed examples.
sessions.contrast: Atwater presents evidence for great past earthquakes. Nelson and colleagues examine how to distinguish coseismic subsidence from processes that also occur on passive coasts. This is refinement of the inference, not a blanket rejection of the discovery.
prompts: Which observations are directly measured and which quantities are reconstructed?
What would make a peat-mud contact insufficient evidence by itself?
What new trace would distinguish competing interpretations?
sessions.prep: Bring a stratigraphic, seismic, or paleoenvironmental interpretation. Separate observations, proxy assumptions, dating uncertainty, and causal claims.
sessions.exercise: Construct an evidence table for suddenness, submergence magnitude, lateral extent, tsunami association, and regional synchrony. Add a plausible nonseismic explanation and identify the additional observation needed to discriminate it.
sessions.output: Trace-inference worksheet: measurement -> uncertainty -> alternative processes -> discriminating trace -> provisional conclusion.
sessions.audit: Replace the repeat Cleland assignment and broad Siever essay with two primary Cascadia papers.

sessions.title: Plate tectonics: concept formation and a discriminating test
sessions.question: How does a new concept make old observations and new measurements jointly discriminating?
reading: Read Wilson in full; sketch the competing slip-direction predictions.
Read Sykes’ abstract, focal-mechanism evidence relevant to transform faults, and conclusions.
sessions.contrast: Wilson’s transform-fault concept enables a specific observational contrast. Sykes uses earthquake mechanisms to examine faulting on oceanic ridges. This is a positive case for hypothesis testing, enabled by concepts and measurement systems that did not arrive from a simple automated loop.
prompts: What was the new conceptual object, not merely the new dataset?
Which result could have counted against the predicted fault motion?
What can these two papers establish about tectonics, and what larger history do they omit?
sessions.prep: Bring an annotated sketch of a ridge-offset geometry and two possible causal interpretations.
sessions.exercise: Build the wider plate-tectonics evidence graph, labeling surveys, instrument advances, models, and tests. Then isolate the Wilson-Sykes link and reconstruct the discriminating prediction without using later consensus as its proof.
sessions.output: Synthesis-agent specification: preserve provenance across datasets, identify shared implications, and state a prediction that separates explanations.
sessions.audit: Replace a broad Dietz retrospective with primary concept-and-test papers. Move the ocean-drilling overview to the field-practice meeting.

sessions.title: New sensing capability versus trustworthy measurement
sessions.question: When does a new sensor change what can be discovered, and what must be established before its numbers count as physical evidence?
reading: Read the main subsea DAS article.
Read the instrument-response study’s calibration approach and discussion; a discussant inspects the response comparisons.
sessions.contrast: The first study demonstrates an observational use of subsea telecom fiber. The second investigates a DAS array’s broadband response. A capability demonstration and a calibration study answer different questions; neither supplies a universal response for every installation.
prompts: What is measured along a fiber, and what is inferred about ground motion?
Could coupling, gauge length, or processing produce a spatial anomaly?
When is improved measurement itself a scientific advance?
sessions.prep: Trace one familiar plotted quantity from physical process to instrument, digitization, calibration, processing, and interpretation.
sessions.exercise: Compare two apparent amplitude anomalies: one caused by a physical change and one by a measurement-chain change. Specify what additional metadata or independent sensor would discriminate them. Do not require the group to implement a DAS simulator during the hour.
sessions.output: Measurement-provenance checklist: observable, units, response, sampling, installation, transforms, uncertainty, and independent checks.
sessions.audit: Replace an indirect seismic-bulletin handbook chapter and a general measurement essay with a concrete geophysical instrument/calibration pair.

sessions.title: Explore freely; distinguish exploration from confirmation
sessions.question: How can we learn from looking at data without misrepresenting a pattern found after inspection as a prediction made beforehand?
reading: Read the opening discussion of data analysis as an empirical activity and selected examples in Tukey; the full 67 pages are optional.
Read Nosek and colleagues in full, concentrating on prediction, postdiction, and transparent separation of analyses.
sessions.contrast: Tukey makes room for data-driven inquiry. Nosek and colleagues argue for clearer evidential status through preregistration. This is a complementary pairing, not exploration versus legitimate science.
prompts: When is a discovered pattern a useful question rather than a confirmed finding?
How do we document previous access to an existing dataset?
What independent evidence is available when laboratory replication is impossible?
sessions.prep: Bring an exploratory figure and list every major choice made after seeing the data. Do not include confidential data in public course materials.
sessions.exercise: Run a paper exercise on the same messy Earth-science dataset: propose plots and candidate questions, then freeze a claim and its test before revealing a reserved period or region. Discuss why spatially or temporally dependent records may make a random row split misleading.
sessions.output: Discovery Agent v0 rubric plus an exploration-to-confirmation handoff: log the exploratory search, freeze the new claim, specify independent evidence, and retain negative outcomes.
sessions.audit: Replace an insufficiently specified edited-volume chapter with a precise methodological paper; preserve exploration rather than demand preregistration of all discovery.

sessions.title: Field and marine research under real constraints
sessions.kind: Local field history / collective observing infrastructure
sessions.question: How do logistics, sampling opportunities, institutions, and irreproducible environments shape the questions scientists can investigate?
reading: Read Powell’s introduction, one field episode, and conclusion.
Read the short scientific-ocean-drilling overview in full.
sessions.contrast: Powell draws on archival and oral-history material; Becker and colleagues give a collective retrospective of an observing program. Compare scales of practice without mistaking a program overview for a contemporaneous shipboard log.
prompts: Which campaign deviations change the scientific interpretation, not just efficiency?
What survives as a reusable sample, measurement, or archive?
How should an agent respond when the planned observation becomes impossible?
sessions.prep: Bring a proposal plan and a nonconfidential account of what actually happened in a lab, field, or marine campaign.
sessions.exercise: Compare planned questions, observations actually obtained, contingencies, revised strategy, and claims ultimately warranted. Introduce one constraint such as lost ship time or an instrument failure and require an explicit scientific tradeoff rather than a silent plan change.
sessions.output: Adaptive observation plan: prioritized evidence, feasible substitutes, provenance of deviations, unanswerable questions, and stopping conditions.
sessions.audit: Keep the close-to-practice Arctic history and pair it with the relocated ocean-drilling paper; remove a general book-chapter substitute.

sessions.title: Serendipity, anomaly, and scientific interestingness
sessions.question: What makes an unexpected observation worth pursuing rather than merely surprising?
reading: Select two discovery episodes from Moore; track the initial problem, surprise, follow-up, and later interpretation.
Read Yaqub’s taxonomy and concluding implications; the discussant examines the archival basis.
sessions.contrast: Moore offers retrospective experience from marine geochemistry. Yaqub distinguishes kinds of serendipity and cautions against assuming it disproves targeted research. An autobiographical success story can illuminate judgment while still being affected by hindsight and selection.
prompts: Would the observation have been recognizable as consequential before its outcome was known?
What distinguishes an artifact from a scientifically productive anomaly?
Can targeted research deliberately preserve room for unanticipated questions?
sessions.prep: Collect several anonymized anomalies from past projects, including artifacts, unresolved observations, and productive surprises.
sessions.exercise: Blind-sort the cases into debug, pursue, connect to another problem, defer, or ignore. Require a next action and an evidence-based reason. Reveal the eventual histories only after the first judgment.
sessions.output: Surprise/interestingness rubric: reproducibility, provenance, conflict with expectations, explanatory reach, follow-up cost, and uncertainty. Reward justified redirection, not anomaly magnitude alone.
sessions.audit: Give Moore a substantive companion rather than treating a first-person narrative as a general theory of discovery.

sessions.title: Hypothesis testing when several models fit
sessions.kind: Limits of validation / practical model comparison
sessions.question: What does a successful model test establish, and what should we do when incompatible models fit the same observations?
reading: Read Oreskes and colleagues in full.
Read Beven and Freer’s equifinality argument and environmental-model example; inspect how acceptable models are retained.
sessions.contrast: The first paper challenges unrestricted truth claims about numerical models of open systems. The second develops an approach to multiple acceptable parameterizations and structures. This is not a claim that software cannot be tested or that predictive skill cannot be assessed.
prompts: What has been tested: code, numerical accuracy, a parameterization, or a causal explanation?
Which independent observable distinguishes the acceptable models?
How do likelihood choices, thresholds, and model inadequacy enter the uncertainty claim?
sessions.prep: Bring two plausible explanations or model configurations for one mature research problem. List shared and differing predictions.
sessions.exercise: Compare an exploration-first workflow with explicit competing models. Define success before seeing their outputs. Use a held-out observable or regime rather than reward an increasingly flexible fit to the same data. Treat GLUE weighting choices explicitly rather than as uniquely determined Bayesian probabilities.
sessions.output: Inquiry-mode routing policy and model-test card: claim, alternatives, measurement assumptions, acceptance criterion, held-out evidence, and conditions for model revision.
sessions.audit: Remove the unfinished companion citation and redundant Platt assignment. Recall Platt from Meeting 1 while using a concrete Earth-system model pair.

sessions.title: Scientific novelty: new to whom, compared with what?
sessions.question: How do people and agents establish what is genuinely new without equating novelty with unfamiliar wording or unusual citation combinations?
reading: Read Uzzi’s main article and identify its operational definition.
Read Fontana’s introduction, validation results, and conclusion; a discussant inspects the physics-paper tests.
sessions.contrast: Uzzi associates citation impact with conventional foundations plus some atypical combinations. Fontana examines whether combination indicators identify novelty rather than interdisciplinarity. The pair supports testing a proxy, not replacing scientific judgment with a distance score.
prompts: What community, corpus, and time define the relevant prior knowledge?
Can a conventional method yield a genuinely new observation?
What should an agent conclude when a search finds no precedent?
sessions.prep: Bring a 150-word contribution claim and two closest precedents. A facilitator prepares anonymous human and agent assessments in advance.
sessions.exercise: Compare a paraphrase of a known result, a new observation with a conventional method, and a conceptual reinterpretation. Audit assessments against the same source packet; then reveal an overlooked precedent and require revision. Distinguish exact, close, and component precedents.
sessions.output: Novelty Dossier v1: atomic claims, novelty types, closest prior art, attempted disconfirmation, search coverage, apparently new component, uncertainty, and separate correctness/value judgments. Track missed novelty, false novelty, prior-art recall, claim localization, calibration, and paraphrase robustness.
sessions.audit: Retain the core pair; place human-review and agent-benchmark papers in optional extensions. A search miss is not proof of historical priority.

sessions.title: Scientific polymathy: breadth, specialization, and borrowed competence
sessions.kind: Historical retrospective / formal argument for specialization
sessions.question: Under what conditions does breadth across fields produce better science than depth in one, and does an agent that supplies competence a researcher does not hold change that answer or only relabel who is borrowing?
reading: Read the chapters covering the age of specialization and Burke's stages of retreat from the polymathic ideal. Ask what a prosopography of roughly five hundred recognized polymaths can and cannot establish: the sample is selected on success, so it does not tell us how often breadth failed.

Read the model and the assumptions it needs. Note the central result: a community can be better off when individuals do not all work on the most promising problem, which makes specialization a collective strategy rather than a loss of ambition.
sessions.contrast: Burke narrates a decline; Kitcher argues that the division of cognitive labor is rational. The pairing asks whether "polymathy declined" and "specialization is optimal" are the same claim in two registers, or genuinely different claims that could come apart. Neither paper concerns agents, which is why they are useful here: they set the terms before the technology is introduced. An agent that supplies borrowed competence either adds a worker to Kitcher's division or changes how much one worker can cover, and those two readings imply different things about what breadth is worth.
prompts: Does a sample of recognized polymaths support any claim about how often breadth fails?
In Kitcher's terms, does an agent add a worker to the division of labor or extend the reach of one?
What would we have to observe in this group to conclude that agent assistance produced real breadth rather than greater confidence outside our competence?
sessions.prep: Bring one project in which you used a method, dataset, instrument, or literature outside your own training. Note who or what supplied that competence, and what check, if any, would have caught an error in it.
sessions.exercise: Take one published paper of your own and list every competence it required: instrument physics, field or shipboard logistics, numerical method, statistics, domain literature, software engineering, and writing. Mark each as held, borrowed from a coauthor, trusted without verification, or absent. Then mark which an agent could plausibly supply today, and for each of those state the specific check that would have caught a wrong answer. Separate the cases where such a check exists from the cases where it does not.
sessions.output: Polymathy Profile v1: a competence inventory using the held / borrowed / trusted / absent categories, a list of substitution candidates, and for each candidate the verification that must exist before delegation is acceptable. Record which verifications the group can actually perform and which are currently aspirational.
sessions.audit: New session added in v0.3. The group's working hypothesis is that agents make individual polymathy practical again; it is entered here as a hypothesis with a stated disconfirming observation, not as a premise. Burke supplies the historical retrospective and Kitcher the argument that specialization is a rational collective strategy rather than a decline, so the pair sets the terms before the technology is introduced.

sessions.title: Scientific advance: cumulative work and field-shaping change
sessions.question: What becomes knowable, explainable, measurable, or possible after a contribution, and can we distinguish that gain from attention or prestige?
reading: Read Wu’s main argument, definition of disruption, and discussion.
Read Petersen’s main critique and conclusions. Two discussants examine the index and reanalysis in depth. Dellsén is optional philosophical framing, not a third required paper.
sessions.contrast: Wu distinguishes developing and disruptive citation patterns and reports associations with team size. Petersen challenges how citation inflation and reference-list properties affect such inferences. Their disagreement concerns measurement as well as interpretation; neither supplies an uncontested scalar measure of scientific progress.
prompts: Can a calibration, correction, archive, or replication be a major advance without an original theory?
Is a “big leap” an intrinsic property or a retrospective judgment about consequences?
How do entry, authority, infrastructure, standards, and funding shape a field?
sessions.prep: Bring one purported turning point and one modest but indispensable contribution. Write a before/after account and initially hide citation counts and journal prestige.
sessions.exercise: Map prior knowledge -> contribution -> new capability -> later questions for both examples. Mark dependencies, uncertainty, and evidence of actual downstream use. Discuss whether apparent transformation depends on many enabling contributions rather than a single paper.
sessions.output: Scientific Advance Profile v1: warranted knowledge/understanding/capability gain, contribution role, users, new tests or questions enabled, dependencies, evidence, time horizon, and uncertainty. Keep prospective promise separate from demonstrated impact.
sessions.audit: Retain the Wu-Petersen methodological pairing as the required pair. Keep progress definitions, gatekeeping, and delayed recognition as optional extensions.

sessions.title: What architecture follows from practice, and what would show it worked?
sessions.kind: Implemented laboratory agent / concrete agent benchmark
sessions.question: Which parts of scientific inquiry are actually delegated in a working agent demonstration, and what evidence would establish that the resulting system improves inquiry rather than scores well on a particular benchmark?
reading: Read the system architecture and one experimental demonstration. Identify which steps the system performed and which a person specified for it.
Read the task construction, evaluation, and stated limitations. The full accepted conference paper and proceedings are linked.
sessions.contrast: Boiko and colleagues demonstrate a tool-using system that acts in a laboratory. ScienceAgentBench specifies executable tasks drawn from published studies and scores them. Between them they cover what an agent is built to do and what a score of its behavior can mean. A demonstration does not establish autonomy across every scientific mode, and success on a supplied analysis task does not by itself evaluate question choice, unexpected discovery, or field-level scientific value.
prompts: Who specified the objective, supplied the tools, and checked the evidence?
Which construct does each proposed metric actually observe, and where could a correct final answer conceal invalid reasoning, leakage, or an unreproducible workflow?
How might a shared automated workflow narrow the questions this group asks, and would our evaluation detect that?
sessions.prep: Bring the inquiry-action vocabulary, exploration policy, measurement-provenance checklist, Novelty Dossier, Scientific Advance Profile, and Polymathy Profile developed earlier. Also bring, if you have them, matched outputs on one task from a human researcher, a hypothesis-first agent, and an inquiry agent, recording model, benchmark, data, tool, and evaluator versions.
sessions.exercise: Draw a state machine with observation, characterization, anomaly follow-up, question formation, competing explanations, testing, and synthesis, and assign evidence requirements to the transitions. Then pick the two transitions the group considers most load-bearing and specify, for each, the test that would show it works: the construct it observes, a positive and a negative control, and the failure it is designed to catch. Note which of those tests the group could actually run this quarter.
sessions.output: Agent Architecture v1 and Scientific Inquiry Benchmark v1, produced together as one artifact so that no capability is specified without the evidence that would check it. The architecture keeps novelty assessment separate from the decision to pursue a project; preserves exploratory, confirmatory, corrective, and infrastructure-building options; and requires traceable tool outputs, explicit uncertainty, and human escalation points. The benchmark names its constructs, tasks, controls, independent evidence, scoring rules, human baseline, run budgets, repeated-run uncertainty, ablations, failure taxonomy, and criteria for improvement.
sessions.audit: Meetings 12 and 13 of v0.2 are merged here in v0.3 to free a slot for polymathy. The required pair is the implemented agent and the concrete benchmark; the two critiques that were previously paired with them, Messeri and Crockett on illusions of understanding and Flake and Fried on measurement, become discussant-led so that the reading load stays at two papers per participant. Both remain listed in the reading library and cited on the page.
